title: What makes an act good (CCC 1750–1756)
hook: the act itself, the intention and the circumstances

segments.voice: Yesterday, called to beatitude: the moral life begins with the happiness a person is made for. Your line was made for happiness. What did you name as your deepest desire? Today closes the week. Day one thousand one hundred thirteen.

Sunday, the collection basket comes down the pew. Three envelopes go in. The first is from a woman who heard the parish is helping a family that lost its home in a fire. The second is from a man who folds his envelope so the person beside him can see how thick it is. The third is from a woman who lost her job last month, and gave anyway, less than she used to. From the back of the church, all three look identical: an envelope, a basket, a hand. But something very different is going on in each one. Today's question sits under all three: what makes an act good?
screen: `THREE ENVELOPES, ONE BASKET.` → `SAME ACT FROM THE BACK PEW.` → `WHAT MAKES IT GOOD?`

segments.voice: The Catechism answers with three things, which it calls the sources of morality. First, the object: what is actually chosen. Giving money, telling the truth, telling a lie. Reason looks at this first, and some acts are wrong whatever the reason behind them. Second, the intention: why. The end a person has in view. One intention can run through a whole string of actions, and one action can carry several intentions at once. Third, the circumstances: who, where, when, how much, under what pressure. Now the rules for how the three fit together, and here the Catechism gets very plain. A good intention can't make a bad act good. Its example is lying: even to help a neighbor, a lie is still a lie. It puts it in one short phrase: the end does not justify the means. It goes the other way too. A bad intention can spoil a good act. The Catechism's example comes straight from Jesus, about giving alms to be seen. In the Douay-Rheims: "sound not a trumpet before thee." The man folding his envelope so the pew can see is doing a good thing for a hollow reason. And circumstances? They can make an act more or less good, more or less serious. Fear, for instance, can lessen a person's responsibility. But circumstances can't turn a wrong act into a right one. So the Catechism's rule is that a good act needs all three together: a good object, a good intention, fitting circumstances. And the third envelope? Thinner than the others, maybe. But the circumstances, a lost job and a tight month, add weight to that gift.
screen: `THE OBJECT: WHAT IS CHOSEN.` · `THE INTENTION: WHY.` · `THE CIRCUMSTANCES: WHO, WHEN, HOW.` · `ALL THREE GOOD TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE END DOES NOT JUSTIFY THE MEANS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one choice by all three. Settle, and breathe. Bring up one decision in front of you this week, small or large. A message to send. Money to spend. A favor to say yes or no to. First, the what: name the act itself, plainly, without the story around it. Then the why: what am I really after here? Be honest, even if the answer is a little embarrassing. Then the when and how: who's affected, what's the timing, what's the pressure? Notice which of the three is the shaky one. If you pray, you can ask for light on that one. The bell holds the time.
What makes an act good. The Catechism names three sources: the act chosen, the intention, and the circumstances, and asks that all three be good together. Today's word.
screen: `WHAT MAKES AN ACT GOOD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what, why, when. This week walked from covenant and the domestic church, through sacramentals, popular piety and funerals, into how Catholics live: called to beatitude, and now what makes an act good. Today, before one choice, ask the three questions. Day one thousand one hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Catholic moral teaching weighs an act by its object, its intention and its circumstances, and some Catholics use those three in an examination of conscience before confession.

myth: a good intention can make any act good
the Catechism says a good intention can't make a bad act good: the end does not justify the means.
a bad intention can spoil a good act
the Catechism's example is giving alms in order to be seen.

they can lessen or increase goodness and responsibility, but can't make a wrong act right.

fork.setup: a coworker made a mistake and asks you to tell the boss a small lie to cover it. your reason is kind: you want to protect her job. what does the Catechism say about that lie?
options: the kind reason makes the lie good.
the lie is still wrong, even with a kind reason.
fork.reveal: the Catechism uses lying as its example: a good intention doesn't make a bad act good. the end does not justify the means.

trapdoor: what you thought: if your heart's in the right place, the act is good.
what it means: the act itself, the intention and the circumstances all count, and a good aim can't rescue a wrong act.
what a scholar hears: the sources of morality, object, end and circumstances, and the old rule that the end does not justify the means.

notes: CCC 1750–1756 paraphrased (copyrighted translation): three sources (1750), object (1751), intention (1752), good intention doesn't justify lying, 'the end does not justify the means', almsgiving for vainglory (1753), circumstances (1754), all three together (1755), some acts wrong regardless (1756). Confirm.
Hook's three envelopes are an invented illustration; the third (a gift after a lost job) shows a circumstance increasing an act's goodness (CCC 1754). A Keeper may prefer a different example.

Editor pass: replaced the third envelope (grocery money, kids going without), which cut against Jesus's praise of the widow's gift and implied a ruling the Catechism doesn't make, with a lost-job gift that circumstances make weightier; trimmed 'fear, ignorance or pressure' to fear, the example CCC 1754 gives.
